extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, newspaper editors, and journalism students (late 19th-century / general audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for producing and running a modern daily newspaper: what to report, how to organize staff, what training and personal qualities journalists need, and the civic responsibilities of the press.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get the news
rubrics_metrics.description: “Get the news, get all the news, and nothing but the news.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dana defines 'news' as everything that occurs and is of human interest or sufficient importance to arrest public attention. He argues against arbitrary limitation of news items and recommends reporting whatever events occur (he even says he would report whatever Divine Providence permitted to occur).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit sources when copying
rubrics_metrics.description: “Copy nothing from another publication without perfect credit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not appropriate others' material. If using material from other publications, give complete and perfect credit—avoid plagiarism and disguise of origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent for interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never print an interview without the knowledge and consent of the party interviewed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain explicit knowledge and consent before publishing interviews to respect subjects and avoid unethical or misleading reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate advertising and news
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never print a paid advertisement as news matter. Let every advertisement appear as an advertisement; no sailing under false colors.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear distinction between editorial content and paid advertisements. Do not disguise ads as news; transparency with readers preserves trust and editorial integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid attacking the weak or defenseless
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never attack the weak or the defenseless, either by argument, by invective, or by ridicule, unless there is some absolute public necessity for so doing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise restraint and proportionality in criticism; attacks on vulnerable targets require clear and compelling public necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate without dogmatism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fight for your opinions, but do not believe that they contain the whole truth or the only truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support positions vigorously but avoid absolutism—recognize limits of one's own viewpoint and foster open-mindedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partisan support with humility
rubrics_metrics.description: “Support your party, if you have one. But do not think all the good men are in it and all the bad ones outside of it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper is partisan, do not succumb to blind partisanship; acknowledge virtue and faults across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain confidence in human progress
rubrics_metrics.description: “Above all, know and believe that humanity is advancing; that there is progress in human life and human affairs; and that, as sure as God lives, the future will be greater and better than the present or the past.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guiding editorial philosophy: a forward-looking optimism that should inform tone and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise patience — do not hurry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Never be in a hurry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care with facts and judgment; haste can cause errors and misjudgments in reporting and editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand by constitutional principles
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hold fast to the Constitution.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defend constitutional governance in reporting and editorial position; respect institutional safeguards and rule of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uphold national symbols/patriotism
rubrics_metrics.description: “Stand by the Stars and Stripes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote civic loyalty and national unity as appropriate for the paper's role; this reflects Dana's late-19th-century exhortation about civic duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice restraint — avoid needless harm
rubrics_metrics.description: “A word that is not spoken never does any mischief.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer restraint when publication would cause needless harm; weigh public interest versus potential damage before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: One serious fault outweighs many goods
rubrics_metrics.description: “All the goodness of a good egg can not make up for the badness of a bad one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single major lapse (ethical, factual, defamatory) can undo accumulated goodwill; maintain consistent standards and correct errors promptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit mistakes
rubrics_metrics.description: “If you find you have been wrong, don't fear to say so.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage transparency and corrections when errors occur; repudiates any tradition of feigned infallibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter must detect truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “The reporter must know the truth when he hears it and sees it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters should develop an instinctive ability to detect deception and verify facts; this honesty/acuity is a prized qualification and foundation for a long career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make reporting vivid and engaging
rubrics_metrics.description: “The invariable law of the newspaper is to be interesting.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even true scientific or dry facts must be reported in a clear, vivid, and interesting manner; tedious truth is ineffective—style and vividness aid retention and public impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist's universal education
rubrics_metrics.description: “The educated newspaper man must be qualified to discuss the questions which the clergyman has to discuss... judge of the science of the physician... rise to those... which make a great lawyer. A journalist must be an all-around man.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should pursue broad, liberal education across disciplines (humanities, sciences, law) to report and judge diverse subjects competently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper office as postgraduate school
rubrics_metrics.description: “The newspaper office is the best post-graduate college that the student of the newspaper profession can have.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical, on-the-job training in a newspaper office is indispensable for learning the craft; college provides foundation but experience is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the language (English + classical roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The first thing... is to know this language [English] thoroughly... without Greek and Latin no man knows English; and without Teutonic no man's knowledge of English is perfect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong command of English, supported by knowledge of classical and Germanic roots, gives a journalist the expressive resources to write precisely and powerfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and rapid information-finding
rubrics_metrics.description: “Accuracy, the faculty of seeing a thing as it is... Next... the ability to know how and where most promptly to look for what you don't know and what you want to know... being able to tell what you know.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue exactness in facts and figures, cultivate research skills for quick verification, and be able to report concisely and precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate critical judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: “The critical faculty, the judgment which... looks at it calmly and says, 'That is true,' or else, 'That is false.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop the instinct and training to assess claims at sight—this mitigates errors and misuse of press power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain business education/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every one of these men... require also a business education. It is only by being put through the mill of business that a man acquires the science of this world.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper personnel (reporters, editors, managers) should understand business realities—advertising, circulation, costs—to run a sustainable paper and make informed editorial-business decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found newspaper upon human nature and audience needs
rubrics_metrics.description: “The newspaper must be founded upon human nature. It must correspond to the wants of the people. It must furnish that sort of information which the people demand, or else it never can be successful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the audience's interests, feelings, and needs; tailor content accordingly while upholding ethical standards—contact with the public is essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize staff with clear roles and trained specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: Dana describes an office with a trained staff of reporters, correspondents, editorial writers, exchange readers, city editor, managing editor, business manager, artists, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign clear, specialized roles (reporters for fieldwork, exchange readers for selecting material, city editor for local news, managing editor for coordination). Invest in trained personnel and adequate resources to sustain a high-quality daily paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor defines the paper's purpose and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: “He [the editor] is the head of the paper; he determines what its purpose shall be... He is the final authority in everything.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial leadership sets mission, political stance, and overall standards; the managing editor enforces timeliness and coordination. Leadership must exercise responsibility and consistent principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the press as a safeguard for liberty and public welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Dana emphasizes the press as the final bulwark against executive ambition and tyranny: a free press preserves liberties and the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the civic function of the press: investigate and criticize power, defend constitutional principles, and act responsibly because of the press's potential influence on public opinion and institutions.
